PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME] and by the Government of the Austrian Republic (“the Government“) on [DATE_TIME], within the [DATE_TIME] time-limit laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 13470/87) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on [DATE_TIME] by a private association with legal personality under [NRP] law, [PERSON] für [PERSON] (OPI). The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government’s application referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48). The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 (art. 10).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant association stated that it wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent it (Rule 30).

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mrs [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43).

As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr [PERSON], acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant association’s representative and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and [DATE_TIME]). Pursuant to the orders made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government’s memorial on [DATE_TIME] and the applicant’s memorial on [DATE_TIME]. The Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing.

On [DATE_TIME] the President granted leave to two non-governmental organisations, “Article 19“ and [PERSON], to submit written observations on specific aspects of the case (Rule 37 para. 1). Their observations were received at the registry on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Commission produced certain documents which the Registrar had sought from it on the President’s instructions.

On [DATE_TIME] the Chamber decided under Rule 41 para. 1 to view the film Das Liebeskonzil, as requested by the applicant. A private showing was held on [DATE_TIME].

In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr [PERSON], Head of the International Affairs Division, Department of the Constitution, Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mr [PERSON], Federal Ministry of Justice, Mr [PERSON], Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Advisers;

for the Commission Mr [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicant association Mr [PERSON], Professor of Law at the University of Innsbruck, Verteidiger in [LOCATION], Counsel. The Court heard their addresses as well as replies to its questions.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. THE PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, [PERSON] für [PERSON] (OPI), is a private association under [NRP] law established in [LOCATION]. According to its articles of association, it is a non-profit-making organisation, its general aim being to promote creativity, communication and entertainment through the audiovisual media. Its activities include operating a cinema called “Cinematograph“ in [LOCATION].

The applicant association announced a series of six showings, which would be accessible to the general public, of the film Das Liebeskonzil (“Council in Heaven“) by [PERSON] (see paragraph 22 below). The first of these showings was scheduled for [DATE_TIME]. All were to take place at [DATE_TIME] except for one matinée performance on [DATE_TIME] at [DATE_TIME] This announcement was made in an information bulletin distributed by OPI to its 2,700 members and in various display windows in [LOCATION] including that of the Cinematograph itself. It was worded as follows: “[PERSON]’s satirical tragedy set in Heaven was filmed by [PERSON] from a performance by [LOCATION] in [LOCATION] and set in the context of a reconstruction of the writer’s trial and conviction in [DATE_TIME] for blasphemy. [PERSON] starts from the assumption that syphilis was God’s punishment for man’s fornication and sinfulness at the time of the Renaissance, especially at the court of the Borgia Pope [PERSON]. In [PERSON]’s film, [PERSON]’s representatives on [LOCATION] carrying the insignia of worldly power closely resemble the heavenly protagonists. Trivial imagery and absurdities of the [NRP] creed are targeted in a caricatural mode and the relationship between religious beliefs and worldly mechanisms of oppression is investigated.“ In addition, the information bulletin carried a statement to the effect that, in accordance with the Tyrolean Cinemas Act ([PERSON]), persons [DATE_TIME] were prohibited from seeing the film. A regional newspaper also announced the title of the film and the date and place of the showing without giving any particulars as to its contents.

At the request of the [LOCATION] diocese of the Roman Catholic Church, the public prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings against OPI’s manager, Mr [PERSON], on [DATE_TIME]. The charge was “disparaging religious doctrines“ (Herabwürdigung religiöser Lehren), an act prohibited by section 188 of the Penal Code (Strafgesetzbuch - see paragraph 25 below).

On [DATE_TIME], after the film had been shown at a private session in the presence of a duty judge ([PERSON]), the public prosecutor made an application for its seizure under section 36 of the Media Act (Mediengesetz - see paragraph 29 below). This application was granted by the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) [DATE_TIME]. As a result, the public showings announced by OPI, the first of which had been scheduled for [DATE_TIME], could not take place. Those who attended at the time set for the first showing were treated to a reading of the script and a discussion instead. As Mr [PERSON] had returned the film to the distributor, the “Czerny“ company in [LOCATION], it was in fact seized at the latter’s premises on [DATE_TIME].

An appeal by Mr [PERSON] against the seizure order, filed with the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), was dismissed on [DATE_TIME]. The Court of Appeal considered that artistic freedom was necessarily limited by the rights of others to freedom of religion and by the duty of the State to safeguard a society based on order and tolerance. It further held that indignation was “justified“ for the purposes of section 188 of the Penal Code only if its object was such as to offend the religious feelings of an average person with normal religious sensitivity. That condition was fulfilled in the instant case and forfeiture of the film could be ordered in principle, at least in “objective proceedings“ (see paragraph 28 below). The wholesale derision of religious feeling outweighed any interest the general public might have in information or the financial interests of persons wishing to show the film.

On [DATE_TIME] the criminal prosecution against Mr [PERSON] was discontinued and the case was pursued in the form of “objective proceedings“ under section 33 para. 2 of the Media Act aimed at suppression of the film.

On [DATE_TIME] a trial took place before the Innsbruck Regional Court. The film was again shown in closed session; its contents were described in detail in the official record of the hearing. Mr [PERSON] appears in the official record of the hearing as a witness. He stated that he had sent the film back to the distributor following the seizure order because he wanted nothing more to do with the matter. It appears from the judgment - which was delivered the same day - that Mr [PERSON] was considered to be a “potentially liable interested party“ ([LOCATION]). The Regional Court found it to be established that the distributor of the film had waived its right to be heard and had agreed to the destruction of its copy of the film.

In its judgment the Regional Court ordered the forfeiture of the film. It held: “The public projection scheduled for [DATE_TIME] of the film Das Liebeskonzil, in which God the Father is presented both in image and in text as a senile, impotent idiot, Christ as a cretin and [PERSON] of God as a wanton lady with a corresponding manner of expression and in which the [NRP] is ridiculed, came within the definition of the criminal offence of disparaging religious precepts as laid down in section 188 of the Penal Code.“ The court’s reasoning included the following: “The conditions of section 188 of the Penal Code are objectively fulfilled by this portrayal of the divine persons - God the Father, [PERSON] of God and Jesus Christ are the central figures in [NRP] religious doctrine and practice, being of the most essential importance, also for the religious understanding of the believers - as well as by the above-mentioned expressions concerning the [NRP], which is one of the most important mysteries of the [NRP] religion, the more so in view of the general character of the film as an attack on [NRP] religions ... ... Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundgesetz) guarantees the freedom of artistic creation and the publication and teaching of art. The scope of artistic freedom was broadened (by the introduction of that article) to the extent that every form of artistic expression is protected and limitations of artistic freedom are no longer possible by way of an express legal provision but may only follow from the limitations inherent in this freedom ... . Artistic freedom cannot be unlimited. The limitations on artistic freedom are to be found, firstly, in other basic rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution (such as the freedom of religion and conscience), secondly, in the need for an ordered form of human coexistence based on tolerance, and finally in flagrant and extreme violations of other interests protected by law ([LOCATION] anderer [PERSON]), the specific circumstances having to be weighed up against each other in each case, taking due account of all relevant considerations ... The fact that the conditions of section 188 of the Penal Code are fulfilled does not automatically mean that the limit of the artistic freedom guaranteed by Article 17a of the Basic Law has been reached. However, in view of the above considerations and the particular gravity in the instant case - which concerned a film primarily intended to be provocative and aimed at the Church - of the multiple and sustained violation of legally protected interests, the basic right of artistic freedom will in the instant case have to come second. ...“

Mr [PERSON] appealed against the judgment of the Regional Court, submitting a declaration signed by some 350 persons who protested that they had been prevented from having free access to a work of art, and claiming that section 188 of the Penal Code had not been interpreted in line with the guarantee of freedom of art laid down by Article 17a of the Basic Law. The Innsbruck Court of Appeal declared the appeal inadmissible on [DATE_TIME]. It found that Mr [PERSON] had no standing, as he was not the owner of the copyright of the film. The judgment was notified to OPI on [DATE_TIME].

The applicants live in [LOCATION].

And you let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept, because when you’ve rented out your arse, you can’t shit when you please.” The newsletter was distributed to staff and displayed on the trade union’s noticeboard on the company’s premises. The employment tribunal observed at the outset that the cause of the dismissal was the content of the newsletter and not the applicants’ trade-union membership. It referred in its judgment to the exercise of the right to freedom of expression in the context of labour relations and to the fact that it was not unlimited. It found that the limits to this right had to be interpreted in accordance with the principle of good faith, which in labour relations had to involve respect for the interests of the employer and the minimum requirements of coexistence in a professional environment. The judgment reiterated the Constitutional Court’s case-law to the effect that the right to respect for freedom of expression was subject to limits derived from labour relations, since the contract of employment created a series of rights and reciprocal obligations that circumscribed the exercise of the right to respect for freedom of expression. For that reason, certain manifestations of this right that might be legitimate in other contexts were not legitimate in the context of labour relations, even though the requirement to act in good faith did not always imply a duty of loyalty to the point of subjecting the worker to the employer’s interests. As to the newsletter’s content, the tribunal took the view that the cartoon and speech bubbles on the cover, together with the articles inside, were offensive and exceeded the limits of freedom of expression and information, impugning the honour and dignity of the human resources manager and of delivery men A. and B., and damaging the image of the company P. Lastly, it noted that the dismissal could not be declared null and void, since it was based on serious misconduct as provided for by law, and found that the applicants’ fundamental rights had not been breached.

The applicants appealed. In a judgment of [DATE_TIME], the High Court of Justice of [LOCATION] upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker’s obligations under the contract and his freedom of expression. The balancing exercise had to enable it to be determined whether or not the reaction of the company that dismissed the employee was legitimate. For the court, the publication of the offending drawing and articles had clearly been harmful to the dignity of the persons concerned and had overstepped the limits of admissible criticism, as the exercise of freedom of expression did not justify the use of insulting, offensive or vexatious expressions that went beyond the legitimate exercise of the right to criticise and clearly impugned the respectability of the persons concerned. The company P. had, moreover, duly shown that the applicants’ dismissal was not a measure of reprisal or punishment, but was based on a genuine, serious and sufficient cause for deciding to terminate their contracts of employment.

The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Supreme Court dismissed their appeal on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of [DATE_TIME], was not pertinent.

Relying on Article 24 (right to a fair hearing) of the Spanish Constitution, and on Articles 20 and 28 taken together (freedom of expression and association), the applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision of [DATE_TIME], served on [DATE_TIME], the Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The decision reads as follows: “... Firstly ... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company because of the judicial proceedings they had brought against it to assert their rights ... Secondly, as to the [alleged] interference with trade-union freedom guaranteed by Article 28 of the Constitution (this complaint incorporating the appellants’ complaint under Article 14 of the Constitution in so far as they alleged discrimination on trade-union grounds), this is inadmissible as [the appellants] have not provided sufficient evidence to show that the company’s action was intended to restrict, hamper or prevent the exercise of their right to freedom of association, on account of their union membership or activities in a trade union. In line with what this court has repeatedly said, such evidence does not consist of a mere allegation of a constitutional violation but must be sufficient for it to be inferred that the violation could have been constituted ... which is not the case here, since the circumstances alleged do not give rise to any suspicion as to the potential violation in question. In their allegations, the appellants have simply expressed their disagreement with the decisions rendered by the courts below, which found in decisions giving reasons and not being manifestly unreasonable that they had committed the acts of which the company had accused them in their letters of dismissal. Thirdly, there has not been a breach of Article 28 § 1 of the Constitution taken together with Article 20 § 1 (a), in the form of an infringement of the appellants’ right to freedom of expression in the context of their union activity, since this fundamental right does not encompass any right to insult others. As the Court held recently in judgment no. [PHONE_NUMBER] of [DATE_TIME] (legal ground 4), reiterating its case-law, although the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions in every circumstance, the constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions which, taking into account the actual circumstances of the case and regardless of their veracity or lack of veracity, are offensive or defamatory and are not pertinent for the purpose of conveying the opinions or information in question. The application of that jurisprudence to the present case leads the Court to the conclusion that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed, since they used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation. [Those cartoons and comments] were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which the appellants wished to complain, and were therefore gratuitous and not necessary for the exercise of freedom of expression in a trade-union context.”

name: Ernst Lughofer
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by Mr [PERSON] Lughofer and Mrs [Person] (“the applicants”), [NRP] nationals, on [DATE_TIME], within the period laid down by former Articles 32 and 47 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It originated in an application (no. 22811/93) against [LOCATION] lodged with the European Commission of Human rights under former Article 25 by the applicants. The applicants’ application referred to Article 48 as amended by Protocol No. 90, which [ LOCATION] had ratified. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants' farm was the object of land consolidation proceedings (Zusammenlegungsverfahren) instituted by the Gmunden District Agricultural Authority. On [DATE_TIME] the District Authority ordered the provisional transfer of the properties concerned, inter alia, land owned by the applicants. The applicants appealed, claiming that they had not received adequate land in exchange for their parcels AK 2 and AK 8. The Upper Austria Regional Land Reform Board (Landesagrarsenat) dismissed the applicants' appeal after an oral hearing held in private, but in the presence of the parties and their lawyer. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint, rejecting at the same time, in accordance with Section 39 (2) no. 6 of the Administrative Court Act.

Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 [DATE_TIME] and in accordance with Article 5 § 4 thereof read in conjunction with Rule 100 § 1 and Rule 24 § 6 of the Rules of Court, a Panel of the Grand Chamber decided on [DATE_TIME] that the case should be dealt with by a Chamber constituted within one of the Sections of the Court.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

In [DATE_TIME] the District Authority issued a consolidation plan (Zusammenlegungsplan). The applicants appealed, claiming that they had not received adequate land in exchange for their parcels AK 2 and AK 8. On [DATE_TIME] the Upper Austria Regional Land Reform Board (Landesagrarsenat) dismissed the applicants' appeal after an oral hearing held in private, but in the presence of the parties and their lawyer.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants filed a complaint with the Administrative Court ([PERSON]) against the above decision. They also asked the Court to hold an oral hearing.

On [DATE_TIME] the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint, rejecting at the same time, in accordance with Section 39 (2) no. 6 of the Administrative Court Act, the applicants' request for an oral hearing.

name: Ekrem Taşçı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43868/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been serving as a non-commissioned officer, was dismissed from the army. The Supreme Military Administrative Court annulled the dismissal decision and accepted the applicant’s compensation claims in part. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The application was dismissed on the grounds of independence and impartiality.

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant, who had been serving as a non-commissioned officer, was dismissed from the army. Subsequently, proceedings were initiated before the Supreme Military Administrative Court to have the decision regarding his dismissal annulled. name: Istvan Herczegfalvy
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] national. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber was constituted ex officio by the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)), who drew by lot the names of the other seven members. The applicant served two prison sentences in succession. He was convicted for assaults on his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials. The Government told him they would not be submitting a memorial. The Court heard addresses by the applicant and his lawyer. The case was heard in public in [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. The proceedings against the applicant were heard by the Court. The applicant was declared partly responsible for the actions of the Government. The hearing was adjourned until a later date. The decision was made to uphold the decision of the Inner Vienna District Court and the Vienna Regional Civil Court. The applicant was declared. incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser (Beistand) for him. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. The applicant was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. He was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could be at risk. The judge ordered Mr [PERSON]’s provisional placement in an institution for mentally ill offenders (Article 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) The Vienna court found the charges against Mr [PERSON] had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] which from [DATE_TIME] at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained, but in prison, on the psychiatrist’s recommendation. The judge ordered that the detention should be continued and that the applicant should be transferred as a matter of urgency to a psychiatric hospital, so that his treatment could be carried out. The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the detention order. The Supreme Court had on [DATE_TIME] varied the judgment of the Review Chamber of the Regional Court in part. Mr Herczegfalvy requested his release but was still detained under Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Regional Court remitted the case to the Supreme Court, which quashed the detention and remitted it. The Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Pursuant to Article 428 (4), the Review chamber and the Court of appeal extended the detention. The applicant was then detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr [PERSON]’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. despite certain improvements there had been no fundamental change in the situation. As the applicant had withdrawn his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing, the judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order (Endverfügung), which set the date of 1 [DATESET] for the next judicial review of the detention. Mr [PERSON] made further applications for release on [DATE_TIME] and [DATED_TIME]. He was conditionally released in accordance with the court’s decision. The court found that the applicant's paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention. He was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM) and was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. The director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below). The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment. Mr [PERSON] went on hunger strike from [DATE_TIME], on which date he allegedly eventually agreed to be fed through a tube (Sondenernährung) once. He later denied that his consent had been validly given. In view of the deterioration of his physical and mental state, he was injected by force with 90mg of [LOCATION] on [Date_TIME] in order to bring about a state of somnolence in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression. While in detention Mr [PERSON] addressed an extremely large number of petitions and complaints to various authorities, relating inter alia to his medical treatment and the proceedings brought by him. As he considered that he did not have the necessary money, he refused on several occasions to put stamps on his letters, or sent them to the Ministry of Justice for that purpose. In order to stem this he sent letters to the relevant authorities, which filled six binders; they were given to him on his discharge. On [DATE_TIME] an expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The Regional Court thereupon refused to release the applicant (see paragraph 22 above) The applicant claims that he was deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention. He alleged that these measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only. The restrictions on access to information were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below), and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion. He was deprived from time to time of writing materials, and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public authorities, in particular the courts. When he left the hospital the applicant was given six binders containing the originals of these letters and also about fifty sealed letters; the postal register showed that the latter had never been sent to their addressees.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] national. The Commission wanted to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, 8, and 13. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The applicant served two prison sentences in succession for assaulting his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials. The Inner Vienna District Court (Bezirksgericht Wien Innere Stadt) and the Vienna Regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für [PERSON) acting as guardianship court declared the applicant partly responsible for the assaults. The Court heard addresses by the applicant, the Government, the Commission and the applicant’s lawyer. The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. In the meantime, further prosecutions were brought against Mr [PERSON] for assaults on warders and fellow prisoners and for serious threats against judges. According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. He was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could be affected. The applicant was transferred to the special prison at [LOCATION], [ LOCATION]. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on [DATE_TIME]. The court found that the charges against Mr [PERSON] had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] as equivalent to a mental illness. The Regional Court, relying on section 50 of the Hospitals Law, ordered that the detention should be continued and that the applicant should be transferred as a matter of urgency to a psychiatric hospital, so that the treatment he required could be carried out. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. On [DATE_TIME] Mr Herczegfalvy requested his release. The investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. At that judge’s request, the psychiatric hospital submitted a report expressing the opinion that it was not possible to place the applicant in ordinary pre-trial detention, as his aggressive behaviour was still causing danger to those around him. The Review Chamber of the Regional Court upheld the detention in issue. Pursuant to Article 429(4), the Review Chamber and the Court of Appeal extended the detention. The Supreme Court quashed the detention order and remitted the case. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr [PERSON]’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. despite certain improvements there had been no fundamental change in the situation. As the applicant had withdrawn his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing, the judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order (Endverfügung), which set the date of 1 [DATED_TIME) for the next judicial review of the detention. Mr [PERSON] was conditionally released on [DATE_TIME] in accordance with the court’s decision. The court found that the applicant's paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention (Haftquerulanz) The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’S appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) of the Criminal Code were not satisfied. The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment, and was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM) The applicant was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. He was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. He then was transferred back to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release. Mr [PERSON] went on hunger strike from [DATE_TIME], on which date he allegedly eventually agreed to be fed through a tube (Sondenernährung) once. He later denied that his consent had been validly given. He stopped refusing food after being allocated a single room and being given some of his files. In view of the deterioration of his physical and mental state, he was injected by force with 90mg of [LOCATION] on [Date_TIME]. Since he had resisted this with violence, the emergency team had had to overpower him. He was transferred to the intensive care unit, as he showed symptoms of pneumonia and nephritis. While in detention Mr [PERSON] addressed an extremely large number of petitions and complaints to various authorities. These letters, which he claimed had not been communicated to the relevant authorities, filled six binders; they were given to him on his discharge. During this period he continued to refuse, at least in part, to take nourishment other than through a tube, but on [DATE_TIME] he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially. A doctor had persuaded him to end his hunger strike by explaining to him that it was endangering his life. After a further series of complaints which were regarded as vexatious, the Regional Court consulted the hospital as to the applicant’s possible release. The Government said the measures were justified for therapeutic reasons. Mr [PERSON] claimed that he had been deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention. He alleged that these measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only. The restrictions on access to information were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below), and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion. The Government said that they had been justified for short-term therapeutic reasons, and that the measures had only been used on a few occasions. The government said that this was not the case and that they would continue to use the measures as a matter of course.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] national, on [DATE_TIME. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [Date_TIME] (art-44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art-46, art-46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8 and 13. The applicant served two prison sentences in succession. He was declared partly responsible for the assault of his wife and clients of his television repair business. The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: Mr [PERSON], Ambassador, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr [ Person], Federal Chancellery, Mrs [Person), Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by them. The proceedings continued until the end of the hearing. The application was rejected. The applicant was found not guilty. The applicant was found. incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser (Beistand) for him. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. He was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could be affected. The applicant was transferred to the special prison at [ LOCATION], [LOCATION]. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant’s appeal against the amended indictment was dismissed by the Court of Appeal. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] as equivalent to a mental illness. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained under Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but in prison, on the psychiatrist”s recommendation. On [DATE_TIME] the Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Applying Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it ordered Mr [PERSON] to be sent to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital so that he could receive urgent medical and socio- and psycho-therapeutic treatment. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal. The Supreme Court quashed the detention order and remitted the case to the Regional Court. Pursuant to Article 429. (4), the Review chamber and the Court of. Appeal extended the detention of Mr Herczegfalvy in question. The applicant was held in a psychiatric hospital in Dusseldorf, Germany. A psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. The Regional Court extended his detention under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested his release, pointing out that the period for carrying out a review of the lawfulness of the detention had expired. The court granted his release subject to supervision. An application to exercise its supervisory jurisdiction (Dienstaufsichtsbeschwerde) was made to the Court of Appeal, which ordered the Regional Court to reach a decision speedily. The latter court ordered a further extension of his detention. Mr [PERSON] had begun a hunger strike as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On [DATE_TIME] he was transferred back to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release. The director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below) The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment. He was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM) Mr [PERSON] again went on hunger strike from [DATE_TIME], on which date he allegedly eventually agreed to be fed through a tube (Sondenernährung) once. However, he later denied that his consent had been validly given. In view of the deterioration of his physical and mental state, he was injected by force with 90mg of [LOCATION] on [Date_TIME), in order to bring about a state of somnolence in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. Since he had resisted this with violence, the emergency team had had to overpower him. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles. While in detention Mr [PERSON] addressed an extremely large number of petitions and complaints to various authorities, relating inter alia to his medical treatment and proceedings brought by him. These letters, which he claimed had not been communicated to the relevant authorities, filled six binders; they were given to him on his discharge. He continued to refuse, at least in part, to take nourishment other than through a tube, but on [DATE_TIME] he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially. A doctor had persuaded him to end his hunger strike by explaining to him that it was endangering his life. Hospital reports had, however, said that he appeared to be adequately nourished. The applicant was deprived from time to time of writing materials and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public. He also claimed that he had been deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention. He alleged that these measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only. According to the Government, these measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law and had been justified for therapeutic reasons. The restrictions on access to information relate to the hospital’s decision to refuse Mr [PERSON] access to the internet for up to three days at a time. They also relate to his treatment at the psychiatric hospital. The hospital management agreed with the applicant that they would be transmitted to him regularly.

PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME], within the [DATE_TIME] period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] national, on [DATE_TIME].

The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, [DATE_TIME] and 13 (art. 3, art. 5-1, art. 5-3, art. 5-4, art. 8, art. 10, art. 13).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr L.-E. [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], substitute judges, subsequently replaced Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], who were unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 para. 1 and 24 para. 1).

Mr [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Austrian Government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant on the organisation of the procedure (Rule 37 para. 1 and Rule 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial, which incorporated his claims for just satisfaction (Article 50 of the Convention) (art. 50), on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Government informed him that they would not be submitting a memorial.

On [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON] gave the applicant leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3).

In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr [PERSON], Ambassador, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr [PERSON], Federal Chancellery, Mrs [PERSON], Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers;

for the Commission Mr [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicant Mr [PERSON], Rechtsanwalt, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by them.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. THE PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

Mr [PERSON] is a [NRP] citizen who has lived in [LOCATION] since [DATE_TIME]. He currently resides in [LOCATION].

A. The proceedings

From [DATE_TIME] to 13 [DATE_TIME] he served two prison sentences in succession, following convictions pronounced by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court ([LOCATION] für [PERSON]) and confirmed in part by the Supreme Court ([PERSON]), inter alia for assaults on his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials.

The Inner Vienna District Court (Bezirksgericht Wien Innere Stadt) on [DATE_TIME] and the Vienna Regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für [PERSON]), acting as guardianship court ([PERSON]), on [DATE_TIME] declared the applicant partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser (Beistand) for him. They did so on the basis of a psychiatrist’s report which had been drawn up following numerous complaints by him about prison conditions. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of [DATE_TIME], his position was equivalent as from [DATE_TIME] to that of a curator ([PERSON]) within the meaning of Article 273 (3), sub-paragraph 3, of the Civil Code (see paragraph 54 below).

In the meantime, further prosecutions were brought against Mr [PERSON] for assaults on warders and fellow prisoners and for serious threats against judges. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court ordered that once he had finished serving his sentence on [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 9 above) the applicant should remain in detention under Article 180 (2), sub-paragraphs 1 and 3, of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 40 below), as there was reason to fear that he might attempt to abscond and might commit other offences. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Regional Court and to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), whose rulings were given on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. The pre-trial detention (Untersuchungshaft) was confirmed by the presiding judge of the Regional Court on [DATE_TIME].

In accordance with the opinions of several experts, the presiding judge on [DATE_TIME] ordered Mr [PERSON]’s provisional placement (vorläufige [PERSON]) in an institution for mentally ill offenders (Article 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; see paragraph 44 below). The order was confirmed by the Review Chamber on [DATE_TIME] and the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME], and the applicant was transferred to the special prison at [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts; he was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could harm his health. Following these reports, the public prosecutor’s office amended the indictment on [DATE_TIME] and now sought Mr [PERSON]’s detention rather than conviction. From that date the detention in issue was based on Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 44 below). The applicant’s appeal against the amended indictment was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME].

The hearing before the Regional Court took place on [DATE_TIME]. It had previously been necessary to adjourn a hearing arranged for [DATE_TIME] because the case-file had been lost, to adjourn a hearing of [DATE_TIME] because of the applicant’s request for further witnesses to be called, a hearing of [DATE_TIME] because the presiding judge was absent, one of [DATE_TIME] because fresh evidence had been produced, one of [DATE_TIME] because of mistakes in sending out summonses, and one of [DATE_TIME] because the applicant had spat in the presiding judge’s face, which had led to the indictment being amended (see paragraph 13 above). On [DATE_TIME] the court found that the charges against Mr [PERSON] had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below), on the grounds that he was dangerous and not criminally responsible for his acts. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] which from [DATE_TIME] at least had been equivalent to a mental illness.

The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained under Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but in prison, on the psychiatrist’s recommendation.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, relying on section 50 of the Hospitals Law, ordered that the detention should be continued and that the applicant should be transferred as a matter of urgency to a psychiatric hospital, so that the treatment he required could be carried out. Mr [PERSON] stayed there from [DATE_TIME] and was then returned to the prison. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on [DATE_TIME] that it had no jurisdiction: as Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was the only provision which could apply, it was for the Review Chamber of the Regional Court to hear the appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] the Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Applying Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it ordered Mr [PERSON] to be sent to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital so that he could receive urgent medical and socio- and psycho-therapeutic treatment there, which was essential inter alia because of the hunger strike he had carried on since [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] he was admitted to ward 23 of that hospital, and stayed there until his release on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME].

In the meantime the Supreme Court had on [DATE_TIME] varied the judgment of [DATE_TIME] in part (see paragraphs 14-15 above), quashed the detention order and remitted the case to the Regional Court.

On [DATE_TIME] Mr Herczegfalvy requested his release. On [DATE_TIME] the investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. At that judge’s request, the psychiatric hospital submitted a report dated [DATE_TIME] expressing the opinion that it was not possible to place the applicant in ordinary pre-trial detention, as his aggressive behaviour was still causing danger to those around him. Pursuant to Article 429 (4), the Review Chamber and the Court of Appeal extended the detention in question in [DATE_TIME].

After hearings on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, to which the case had been remitted (see paragraph 18 above), found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy - which included further serious threats against a judge on [DATE_TIME] - had been proved and ordered him to be detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. It based its decision on the judgment of [DATE_TIME], the three psychiatric reports on which it had been based (see paragraph 14 above), and the opinions of the authors of the reports, who had appeared at the hearing and stated that despite certain improvements there had been no fundamental change in the situation. As the applicant had withdrawn his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing on [DATE_TIME] and at a hearing on [DATE_TIME], the judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order (Endverfügung), which set the date of 1 [DATE_TIME] for the next judicial review of the detention (Article 25 (3) of the Criminal Code; see paragraph 46 below). The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to [LOCATION], which was discussed on [DATE_TIME] but did not come about.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr [PERSON]’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. The court took its decision under Article 25 (3) of the Criminal Code, after an official of the psychiatric hospital had stated to the court that the [DATE_TIME] review of the lawfulness of the detention should have taken place on [DATE_TIME] at the latest (see paragraph 20 above).

On [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and a date in [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested his release, pointing out that the period for carrying out the [DATE_TIME] review had expired on [DATE_TIME]. On receiving the first of these applications, the court consulted a psychiatrist, who submitted a report on [DATE_TIME] recommending the applicant’s release subject to supervision (see paragraph 33 below). An application to exercise its supervisory jurisdiction (Dienstaufsichtsbeschwerde) was made to the Court of Appeal, which ordered the Regional Court to reach a decision speedily; on [DATE_TIME] the latter court ordered a further extension of the detention in issue. Taking into account the opinions of the psychiatric expert and the director of the hospital, filed on [DATE_TIME], it considered that there had been no fundamental change in Mr [PERSON]’s mental state. He was still suffering from paranoia [NRP], and if released would undoubtedly refuse to follow the necessary course of treatment; he would consequently be likely to bring numerous complaints or even carry out the threats he had made, in particular those against the prison staff (see paragraph 33 below). On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) of the Criminal Code were not satisfied.

Mr [PERSON] made further applications for release on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. He was conditionally released on [DATE_TIME] in accordance with the court’s decision of [DATE_TIME], itself based on a psychiatric report dated [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 34 below). The court found that the applicant’s paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention (Haftquerulanz); the vexatious complaints and petitions (Rechtsquerulanz) did not constitute a danger within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code; since being detained the applicant had behaved with genuine aggressiveness on a few occasions only; although the possibility could not be excluded of his becoming aggressive in the event of frustration, his psychiatric history did not permit the conclusion that his abnormal personality would induce him to commit criminal offences; moreover, continued psychiatric treatment or treatment by drugs was not considered necessary by the expert, although it was recommended.

B. The medical treatment

On being returned to prison after his stay in the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital from [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 16 above), Mr [PERSON] had begun a hunger strike on [DATE_TIME] as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on [DATE_TIME] and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On [DATE_TIME] he was transferred back to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 23 above).

As the applicant was in an extremely weak state when returned there, the director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below). The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment, and was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM); on [DATE_TIME] he was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. On [DATE_TIME] he was given a different neuroleptic (Sordinol IM), as infiltrations had appeared. He stopped refusing food on [DATE_TIME], after being allocated a single room and being given some of his files.

Mr [PERSON] again went on hunger strike from [DATE_TIME], on which date he allegedly eventually agreed to be fed through a tube (Sondenernährung) once [DATE_TIME]. However, he later denied that his consent had been validly given.

In view of the deterioration of his physical and mental state, he was injected by force with 90mg of [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME], in order to bring about a state of somnolence ([LOCATION]) in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. Since he had resisted this with violence, the emergency team had had to overpower him. On [DATE_TIME] he was transferred to the intensive care unit, as he showed symptoms of pneumonia and nephritis; he stayed there until [DATE_TIME].

He had not made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making; the restraints were not removed until [DATE_TIME]. According to the Government, their position was changed regularly, in order to avoid nervous paralysis, and on [DATE_TIME] he had agreed to be fed by a woman doctor. The applicant stated, however, that other belts had been put around his thighs and stomach and had been untied for the first time only on [DATE_TIME]; in order to obtain his files and writing materials with which to write his complaints, he had continued his hunger strike without interruption, and had been artificially fed throughout this period.

From [DATE_TIME] the applicant calmed down and behaved in a more co-operative manner. Although he continued to insult the staff from time to time, he agreed to communicate with those around him and consented to being fed through a tube by a female doctor twice [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] he was given paper and a ballpoint pen.

Following a dispute about his correspondence, Mr [PERSON] was forbidden on [DATE_TIME] to watch television. As his physical resistance to the forced administration of neuroleptics had frequently been in vain and had even led to injuries (loss of teeth, broken ribs and bruises), he brought a complaint of assault on each occasion that he was given medicaments. These letters, which he claimed had not been communicated to the relevant authorities, filled six binders; they were given to him on his discharge.

During this period he continued to refuse, at least in part, to take nourishment other than through a tube, but on [DATE_TIME] he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially, as a doctor had persuaded him to end his hunger strike by explaining to him that it was endangering his life. Hospital reports had, however, stated that he appeared to be adequately nourished.

In an opinion of [DATE_TIME] an expert considered that conditional release of the applicant would be possible if certain accompanying psychiatric and social measures were taken. In his view, Mr [PERSON]’s behaviour was much improved, so that there was now virtually no danger.

After a further series of complaints which were regarded as vexatious, the Regional Court consulted the hospital on [DATE_TIME] as to the applicant’s possible release. On [DATE_TIME] an expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code. However, in a letter of [DATE_TIME], the director of the hospital advised the court not to terminate Mr [PERSON]’s detention; as the treatment carried out, based on medication, had only a sedative effect, the possibility could not be excluded that if he were released, he would again become aggressive and dangerous. The Regional Court thereupon on [DATE_TIME] refused to release the applicant (see paragraph 22 above).

He eventually recovered his liberty on [DATE_TIME], after a further expert report dated [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 23 above).

C. The control of correspondence

While in detention Mr [PERSON] addressed an extremely large number of petitions and complaints to various authorities, relating inter alia to his medical treatment and the proceedings brought by him. As he considered that he did not have the necessary money, he refused on several occasions to put stamps on his letters, or sent them to the Ministry of Justice for that purpose. In order to stem this flow of correspondence, he was deprived from time to time of writing materials, and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public authorities, in particular the courts.

With respect to the letters written at the psychiatric hospital, the hospital management had agreed with the applicant’s curator that they would be transmitted to him regularly and it would be for him to decide whether it was necessary to send them on; this system would apply to all letters other than those to his lawyer, his adviser and the guardianship court. Mr [PERSON] has complained that even those letters were not all sent on.

When he left the hospital the applicant was given six binders containing the originals of these letters and also about fifty sealed letters; the postal register showed that the latter had never been sent to their addressees, namely the police, the public prosecutor’s office and the courts.

D. The restrictions on access to information

Mr [PERSON] also claimed that he had been deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention, in particular from [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME] and from [DATE_TIME]; from [DATE_TIME] there had been no television set in his cell or in the ward. He alleged that these measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only.

According to the Government, these measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below), had been justified for therapeutic reasons, and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35968/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that [NRP] court decisions refusing her claims for reimbursement of gender reassignment measures and also the related proceedings were in breach of her right to a fair trial. The case was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Chamber declared the application admissible. The court found that the conditions under section 1. of the Transsexuals Act (Gesetz über die [LOCATION] und die Feststell) were met. The applicant, represented by counsel, brought an action with the Berlin Regional Court against a [NRP] health insurance company. Having been affiliated to this company since [DATE_TIME], she claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. She further requested a declaratory judgment to the effect that the defendant company was liable to reimburse 50% of the expenses for gender reassignment operations. The court found that the experts had convincingly shown that the applicant had been under the constraint of living according to these tendencies and that there was a high probability that the she would not change these tendencies in the future. The judge ruled that her transsexuality had to be regarded as a disease. The court considered that under the relevant provisions of the General Insurance Conditions (Allgemeine Versicherungsbedingungen) governing the contractual relations between the applicant and her private health insurance company, the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement of medical treatment regarding her transsexuality. The court was not convinced that, on account of the applicant’s resistance to therapy, the intended operation was the only possible treatment. The Regional Court found that the evidence did not show conclusively that the gender reassignment measures would relieve the applicant's physical and mental difficulties, a further criterion for assuming their medical necessity. The expert Dr [PERSON] had merely recommended the operation from a psychiatric-psychotherapeutic point of view, as it would improve her social situation. The Court of Appeal valued the claims at stake at 28,455.92 German marks. The applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that, according to the opinion of the expert Dr [PERSON], her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. The expert had considered gender reassignment surgery as one possible medical treatment; however, the question of necessity could not be clearly affirmed given the diverging scientific opinions and results. The court had not, therefore, been required, of its own motion, to summon the expert to explain his opinion orally. In the applicant’s case, the advantages of an operation would prevail, while psychotherapy could not cure the transsexuality on account of the applicant's chronic narcissistic character structure. The Court of Appeal added that, while the expert had mentioned that the gender reassignment operation ‘formed part of the curative treatment of a mental disease’, he had regarded success as rather uncertain. Such a vague hope could not justify the necessity of medical treatment, bearing the aim of health insurance in mind. The applicant had therefore failed to prove that the conditions for reimbursement were met in her case. In any event, the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement under clause 5.1(b) of the General Insurance Conditions on the ground that she had herself deliberately caused the disease, as argued by the defendant in earlier submissions. The German Transsexuals Act (Gesetz über die [LOCATION] und die Feststellung der Geschlechtszugehörigkeit in besonderen Fällen) of [DATE_TIME) was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The case was decided on the grounds of the right of the applicant to be transsexual. The court ruled in favour of the transsexual, and the decision was upheld on appeal. The appeal was heard before the European Court of Human Rights, in Strasbourg. Under section 1 of the Transsexuals Act, persons may request that their forenames be changed if, on account of their transsexual orientation, they no longer feel they belong to the sex recorded in the register of births.
